review: Loved these games as a kid, some of my favorites. Glad they got it working on Steam for modern systems.

Sorry to say but the combat is garbage in all of these games, even the fan remake of 2 which most consider has the best combat. Yikes. It's clunky, boring, frustrating, and highly repetitive. I know said fan remake of 2 lets you turn down the combat difficulty, but I don't think the other games let you. But even if they do, combat is a big point of these games and we sacrifice some of the puzzle gameplay of other PnC games of the era to have it. So making it a non-issue gives you a watered down game from both sides: the combat and puzzles. So you're left with games that have crappy combat and mediocre point and click gameplay. Play an action game for combat, and play other sierra classics like King's Quest for the PnC.

Instead play Mage's Initiation and Quest for Infamy, both of which have combat similar to QfG but tolerable, and better PnC gameplay.

If you really want to check these games out, playing them in Scummvm is a must. Be sure to enable fullscreen in its settings so the resolution isn't tiny. There's also fan patches for games 3-5 and the aforementioned fan remake of 2 so those are a must. Only 5 can't be played in scumm so you're forced to deal with its low res.

Other than that the characters and such are cool, especially the Katta people.

From the whole pack, the standout adventures are Quest for Glory I (the enhanced VGA remake), III, and IV, each capturing the series’ unique blend of humor, mystery, and fantasy.

It’s hard to pin down exactly what genre these games belong to. You get to freely roam the world using a point-and-click adventure system, while RPG mechanics and combat stats have a strong impact depending on your chosen class - Fighter, Mage, or Thief. There’s even a special Paladin class for players who import their save files across games, a brilliant touch of continuity.

The world itself changes dynamically between day and night. While the overall story remains unified, each class offers unique paths and quests, allowing you to experience additional content and piece together the full picture.

It’s a timeless experience that rewards curiosity, creativity, and a little persistence, a true classic by Corey and Lori from the golden era of Sierra adventures.

So in practical terms, this one is worth getting on sale in order to play through QFG1&4. You could use a walkthrough, and then replay with one of the other two classes. The games are two of the relatively many gems of the 1990s that still play fine 30 years later.

“Quest for Glory” series of 5 games is a true classic from the 90s, a unique blend of point&click adventure and RPG. At the beginning you choose one of the three classes – fighter, mage or thief (and starting QfG3 also paladin); distribute skill points to your attributes (with an opportunity to create a hybrid class, like spellcasting thief), and then set out into the fantasy world to prove yourself a true hero. Game features classic adventuring elements like picking items and using them, solving problems that are heavily influenced by your class (e.g. when faced with a locked door, fighter will force it open, mage will use opening spell, and thief will pick the lock), and attributes determining your chance of success. The other facet is combat, with system that is a bit... adventurish, but it serves its purpose: kill monsters, improve skills, get loot, buy more stuff. Graphics are typical Sierra style, ranging from original EGA of the first two games (collection contains also VGA conversion of the first game, and for second you can download it for free from AGD Interactive), to classic and beautiful-looking VGA for third and fourth, to not very well executed attempt at 3D style in the fifth. QfG games were very popular among adventure players when they first came out, but younger players who enjoy retro games will undoubtedly find them entertaining as well.

I can't count how many hours I played these games before needing to buy them again on Steam so they would work on my modern computer. They're perfect examples of what Sierra Games was capable of during its heyday. Goofy humor, original takes on otherwise tired tropes and mechanics, settings that are inspired by different cultures and their mythologies, and engaging stories.

The first four are all point-and-click adventures with some RPG elements while the fifth is much more action-oriented. Sadly it also introduces the frustrating mechanic of any helmet and armor heavier than enchanted leather impacting some attributes and the Magic skill when it was never present before. The hidden fourth class, the paladin, is basically a fighter with a healing power and danger sense (until the fifth game greatly expanded the abilities) as well as the ability to acquire and use a magic sword that does the most (again, until the fifth game) damage in combat.

Final saves from previous games can be imported to the sequels, allowing you start with a character with better skills and attributes or even abilities their class wouldn't normally have (magic, the ability to sneak and pick locks, etc.). You can also find utilities to create such import files and even saves ready for import online. The one exception is the final save for QFG 5, explained below.

My one and only complaint? Sierra went out of business before the sixth game, based on India and Hindu mythology, could be made. We never got the chance to fly Wolfie back to his native Punjab.
